# Getting Started with R {#sec-getting-started-with-r}

::: {.guiding-question}
Guiding question: **How do I install R and learn enough of its syntax to follow this module's code?**
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## By the end of this chapter you will be able to:
1. **Install** R on your own computer.
2. **Run** a line of code in the R console and read its output.
3. **Recognise** the core syntax used throughout this module: assignment (`<-`), function
   calls, vectors and the pipe (`%>%` / `|>`).
4. **Install** an R package and load it with `library()`.
:::

*(Source materials: DataCamp, Hands-On Programming with R, swirl — see [Resources](resources.qmd).)*

## Who This Chapter Is For

Chapters 1–8 all assume you can already run R code and read what it prints back — they
teach data analysis *with* R, not R itself. If you have never written a line of R before,
start here rather than at [Chapter 1](01-understanding-data.qmd). This chapter and
[Rubric 10](10-getting-started-with-rstudio.qmd) build exactly the foundation you need,
without requiring you to already know any statistics — that part comes later.

If you already have R installed and have written at least a little R or another
programming language before, skim this chapter for anything unfamiliar and move on to
[Rubric 10](10-getting-started-with-rstudio.qmd) or straight to [Chapter
1](01-understanding-data.qmd).

## Installing R

**R** is a free, open-source language and environment for statistical computing. Download
it from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/), the official R repository, and pick the
installer for your operating system (Windows, macOS or Linux). Accept the default
options during installation — nothing here needs customising for this module.

R on its own gives you a very plain console window. [Rubric
10](10-getting-started-with-rstudio.qmd) covers **RStudio**, the friendlier interface this
module's instructions assume you're using — install R first, then RStudio.

## Learning the Basics

Rather than duplicating a full introduction to R here, this module points you to
**[DataCamp's "Data Analyst with R" career track](https://app.datacamp.com/learn/career-tracks/data-analyst-with-r)**,
an interactive, browser-based course that teaches R hands-on, no prior programming
experience assumed. You don't need to complete the whole track before moving on — the
early "Introduction to R" course is enough to follow Chapters 1–4.

As you work through it, pay particular attention to the handful of concepts that recur
constantly in this module's own code:

- **Assignment** (`<-`): `x <- 10` stores the value `10` in a variable named `x`. You'll
  see this on nearly every line.
- **Function calls**: `mean(x)`, `read_csv("file.csv")` — a function name followed by its
  arguments in parentheses.
- **Vectors and data frames**: a vector is an ordered list of values of the same type; a
  data frame is a table — rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. Every dataset you touch in
  this module is a data frame.
- **The pipe** (`%>%` from the `tidyverse`, or base R's `|>`): reads as "and then" — it
  takes what's on its left and feeds it as the first argument into what's on its right, so
  a sequence of steps reads top to bottom instead of nested inside-out. [Chapter
  2](02-exploring-visualizing.qmd) introduces it again with a conveyor-belt analogy, once
  you have real data to use it on.

::: {.exercise-box}
### Exercise 9.1 — Install R and run your first commands

1. Install R from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/) for your operating system.
2. Open R (or, once you've also read [Rubric 10](10-getting-started-with-rstudio.qmd),
   RStudio) and, in the console, type `2 + 2` and press Enter.
3. Create a variable: type `x <- 10`, press Enter, then type `x` on its own and press
   Enter again — R should print `10`.
4. Install the package this module uses throughout: `install.packages("tidyverse")`, then
   load it with `library(tidyverse)`.

**Reflect:** what did the console print after each step, and did it match what you
expected?
:::

::: {.differentiation-box}
::: {.struggling}
If reading someone else's R code still feels like reading a foreign language: start with
[DataCamp's free "Introduction to R" course](https://app.datacamp.com/learn/career-tracks/data-analyst-with-r)
specifically rather than the full career track, and don't move on until variables,
vectors and function calls feel ordinary. [swirl](https://swirlstats.com/students.html)'s
"R Programming" module is a good companion — short, interactive exercises that run
directly in your own R console, so you learn by doing rather than reading.
:::
::: {.deeper}
If you'd rather work from a short, structured book than an interactive course:
[Hands-On Programming with R](https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/) starts from
absolute zero and builds toward writing your own small functions and simulations.
:::

## Check Your Understanding

- Do you have R installed and running on your own computer?
- Can you explain, in your own words, what `<-` does?
- Given a short function call like `mean(x)`, could you say what it does even without
  having seen that exact function before?
- Do you know how to install and load an R package?
